claims.text: Superconductivity in Ti-Nb-Mo-Cr-W high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the density of states at the Fermi level.
Substituting Cr with V adjusts the alloy's valence electron count.
Changing the valence electron count through V substitution modulates the density of states at the Fermi level.
Rapid melt-quenching followed by homogenization annealing can produce a homogeneous Ti-Nb-Mo-Cr-W solid solution.
Incremental replacement of Cr by 5-20 at.% V will systematically alter the alloy's electronic structure.
Identical processing and annealing conditions will help maintain a uniform solid solution and avoid phase separation across the alloy series.
V substitution causes subtle changes in local bonding environments.
Changes in local electronic structure and bonding modify the density of states at the Fermi level.
Under BCS theory, electron-phonon coupling strength is sensitive to the density of states at the Fermi level.
Electron-phonon coupling strength affects the superconducting transition temperature.
V-induced changes in the density of states affect the electron-pairing interaction responsible for superconductivity.
The superconducting transition temperature will vary non-monotonically with increasing V content.
An optimal electron count will produce a peak transition temperature relative to the Ti-Nb-Mo-Cr-W baseline.
Secondary-phase formation or significant chemical ordering may introduce effects on superconductivity beyond the proposed density-of-states mechanism.
Changes in phonon modes and local structure may compensate for the effects of density-of-states changes on the transition temperature.
Photoemission or tunneling spectroscopy can probe changes in the density of states at the Fermi level in the alloy series.
Failure to observe the predicted non-monotonic transition-temperature trend would falsify the stated hypothesis.
